title: Case Study: YouTube / Netflix Video Streaming
summary: Design a global video streaming platform like YouTube or Netflix capable of ingesting massive video uploads, transcoding them instantly, and streaming 4K video to millions of concurrent users without buffering.

explanation.overview: A video streaming platform is a fundamentally different system design challenge compared to standard web apps. It requires handling massive, unpredictable payloads (Uploads), intensive CPU-bound processing (Transcoding), and globally distributed static asset delivery (CDN). The architecture splits into a Control Plane (handling user metadata, search, comments) and a Data Plane (handling the actual bytes of the video files).
explanation.how_it_works_internally: INTERNAL Mechanics: When a user uploads a video, they do not send 5GB through your API Gateway. Instead, the server generates a Pre-Signed URL allowing the client to upload chunks directly to a Blob Storage bucket (AWS S3) using multi-part upload. Once the upload finishes, an Event Notification triggers a Kafka queue. A fleet of Worker Nodes consumes this queue to perform Video Transcoding, converting the raw file into Dash/HLS streams at various resolutions (1080p, 720p, 480p). Finally, these processed chunks are replicated to global CDNs. When a viewer clicks play, their client downloads an index file (Manifest) and begins pulling chunks directly from the nearest CDN edge node.

step_by_step.title: Multi-part Direct Upload
step_by_step.detail: Client requests an upload token. Server returns a signed S3 URL. Client uploads a 2GB file in 5MB chunks directly to storage, entirely bypassing the web servers.

step_by_step.title: Asynchronous Transcoding Pipeline
step_by_step.detail: S3 triggers an event to Kafka. Transcoder workers pull the video, split it by timeframes (e.g., 10-second segments), and process them in parallel across hundreds of cores.

step_by_step.title: Adaptive Bitrate Streaming (ABR)
step_by_step.detail: The transcoder outputs a manifest file (M3U8). The client downloads this file and continuously monitors its own network speed. If the network drops, the client seamlessly requests lower resolution chunks from the CDN.

step_by_step.title: Metadata Database Scaling
step_by_step.detail: While video files live in S3/CDN, metadata (Title, Description, Likes) lives in a Sharded RDBMS (e.g., Vitess/MySQL) to support complex ACID transactions and search indexing.

key_concepts.definition: INTERNAL: A cryptographic signature generated by the backend granting a client temporary, restricted access to upload directly to a third-party storage provider (S3). Prevents the backend from becoming an I/O bottleneck.

A globally distributed network of proxy servers deployed in multiple data centers. Their goal is to serve content to end-users with high availability and high performance by caching video chunks physically near the user's ISP.

examples.title: Python Implementation Snippet: Transcoding Worker
examples.description: Concrete Python code proving how to trigger asynchronous FFmpeg video compression on a worker node.
examples.code:
import subprocess
import boto3

def transcode_segment(s3_input_key, s3_output_bucket, resolution):
    # Download chunk from S3
    download_from_s3(s3_input_key, 'input.mp4')
    
    # Execute FFmpeg via subprocess to enforce strict CPU limits
    cmd = ['ffmpeg', '-i', 'input.mp4', '-vf', f'scale=-1:{resolution}', '-crf', '23', 'output.mp4']
    subprocess.run(cmd, check=True)
    
    # Upload transcoded chunk to edge origin
    output_key = s3_input_key.replace('.mp4', f'_{resolution}p.mp4')
    boto3.client('s3').upload_file('output.mp4', s3_output_bucket, output_key)
    return output_key

examples.title: Decision Matrix & Tradeoffs: Streaming Protocols
examples.description: Evaluating how to deliver video over the internet.
examples.code:
OPTION RTMP vs OPTION HLS/DASH
------------------------------
Pros RTMP: Extremely low latency (1-3 seconds), good for live streaming (Twitch).
Cons RTMP: Requires a persistent connection, easily blocked by firewalls, does not work efficiently over standard CDNs.
Pros HLS: Runs over standard HTTP port 80/443, naturally cached by all CDNs, supports adaptive bitrate.
Cons HLS: High latency (10-30 seconds). (YouTube relies primarily on MPEG-DASH).

configurable_params.name: Library Configuration Parameters (Kafka Consumer)
configurable_params.effect: Modify parameter `max.poll.interval.ms = 3600000` (1 hour) for transcoding workers.
configurable_params.tradeoff: Transcoding a 4K video takes massive time. If the poll interval is too short, Kafka assumes the worker died, reassigns the partition, and causes infinite duplicate processing pipelines.

advanced_tweaks.when_to_use: Handling client view-counters and resume-playback state.
advanced_tweaks.how: View counts cannot be synchronously updated in an RDBMS per view. The stateless Web Servers drop view events onto a Kafka topic. A streaming Analytics engine (Flink) aggregates views in memory every 5 seconds and flushes the bulk state `UPDATE video SET views = views + 400` to the database.

limitations: Storage Costs: Storing 4K video in 5 different formats is astronomically expensive. TWEAK: Only transcode popular videos into 4K immediately. For long-tail (rarely viewed) videos, only store 720p. If a video goes viral, trigger an asynchronous upscale/transcode to 4K dynamically.

Global Replication Delay: A video uploaded in Tokyo might take minutes to replicate to a CDN in New York. TWEAK: Serve the video directly from the core S3 bucket while replication is in-flight, accepting temporary higher latency for instant availability.

technologies_used.details: YouTube created Vitess (a database clustering system for horizontal scaling of MySQL) to handle massive metadata scaling. It abstracts the routing logic so the application code interacts with what looks like a single massive database, while Vitess handles sharding underneath.
